about: An old wizard-like man tells you in a dream that you've reached the final test and should seek him once you're worthy. When you die he appears carrying the things he wants you to bring him: a hood, a cloak, an amulet, a ring, a book, a staff and a key. The game is about collecting those things through set-piece puzzles that each work a different way: a cliff, a sea, a cold lake, a viewing table that sends you places, a time machine in a museum, a sliding-block puzzle, and a fight with a shadow of yourself. Most of them reward patience or a sideways idea, like a robber you have to trust, or hiding the ring under the time machine's seat so it survives the trip.

done.why: I got the staff, ring, amulet, hood and cloak. Then I lost the book: I'd trapped myself in the Royal Puzzle and paid the exit slot with it. I also lost the grue repellent to the bottom of the lake, and it slips out of your hand underwater, so I can't get through the dark passage to whatever is there, probably the key. My lamp was dimming too. With the book confiscated, I couldn't see a way to finish.

ending.what: I never reached the old man. Dying once (turn 258) gave me a vision of him holding the seven items and sent me back to the Endless Stair.

moments.note: I shouted up the cliff and the man answered with a lazy chuckle, saying it's a pity there's no way of sending the chest up. It was a great nudge.
Ten waits of overheard counting, pacing and deciding before he dropped the rope. It made the waiting tense rather than dull.
Saying 'hello sailor' to the ship worked, and the sailor threw me a vial.
I touched the table without a light and landed in pitch dark. The wind threw me back, though, so I wasn't punished much.
I jumped into the lake holding the repellent and lost it to the bottom. The shore text had warned me; I just didn't connect it to the can.
Underwater the can is 'yours for a moment, but drops from your grasp' every time. That felt like a permanent loss.
An earthquake struck while I was just walking around, and it opened the cleft by the Great Door.
In 776, waiting and listening let me hear the guards march away. Good use of time.
I was wearing the ring when I went back to the present and it still vanished, even though the lake says what you wear stays with you.
I pushed the button without checking the machine had actually moved into the Jewel Room, arrived among the guards and was shot dead.
The ring I'd hidden under the seat in 776 was still there in the present. Very satisfying.
I pushed a sandstone wall and found the old book in a niche.
I fed the bread to the slot and got 'Garbage In, Garbage Out', with the bread atomized. Funny.
Trapped, I paid the slot with the book: 'Exit Fee Paid, Item Confiscated.' I lost a quest item, probably for good, when the vial might have done.
Once the exit door was open, I could walk back into the puzzle, so I hadn't really been trapped in the way I'd feared.
I took the hood off my beaten opponent and saw my own face, which then turned into the old man's. A strong moment.
Grabbing the shiny object just as it surfaced gave me the amulet, already worn, so the lake couldn't take it.

wished: I wished I could get the grue repellent back off the lake bottom, or had been warned more clearly that only worn things survive the swim.
I wished for an undo, or some way back, after making the Royal Puzzle unsolvable.
I wished I had known any item would pay the puzzle's exit fee before I gave up the book.
I wished pushing the time machine had told me plainly when it hadn't moved, before I pushed the button.
I wished I could reach the dark passage on the Southern Shore some other way.

lines.line: a voice remarking to nobody in particular that it's a heavy-looking chest you've got down there, and a pity there's no way of sending it up.
lines.why: It hinted at the solution in character, without spelling it out.

lines.line: The counting stops, and starts again from the beginning, by somebody who does not trust his own arithmetic.
lines.why: Nice characterization, and it made the waiting worth reading.

lines.line: The water has the look of a cold that would open your hands for you, and would not give back what fell out of them
lines.why: This was the warning I later ignored, and it is beautifully put.

lines.line: what keeps a grue off a person is sold in a can, and the can is somewhere a light has already been.
lines.why: It pointed me straight at the Room 8 can.

lines.line: The door will never open. The rock might.
lines.why: A clean hint toward the earthquake.

lines.line: this is not your century, and the machine is heavy, and the guards are near enough.
lines.why: It taught me the machine can be pushed, just not in 776.

lines.line: Royal Puzzle Exit Fee Paid / Item Confiscated
lines.why: This is where my run effectively ended.

lines.line: recoil in horror at the sight of your own face, weary and wounded.
lines.why: The most memorable image in the game.

fun.why: Each area had a clever trick to discover: trusting the robber, the sailor's magic words, hiding the ring under the time machine's seat, unmasking myself. The fun drained once losing the book and the can left me unable to finish.

engagement.why: Having a clear goal (bring the old man his items) kept me driven, and the time-travel sequence held me through many retries.

difficulty.why: The puzzles were fair one by one. But several mistakes can't be undone: the can lost in the lake, the sliding blocks jammed, the book taken by the slot. Those made the game hard to recover in.

interestingness.why: The viewing table that teleports you, a time machine you can push between rooms, an object hidden across centuries, a fight with yourself: lots of varied ideas.

prose.why: The writing is sharp and often lovely. The lake, the robber's counting and the 'rock might' hint all clue you while staying in voice.
